title: Station Meridian Rising Again
premise: Edmund Blackwood, a xenolinguist stripped of the ability to dream in human tongues, ferries cargo along a dying trade route and stumbles on a name that should not exist: a passenger aboard a ship that was decommissioned before launch. The trail leads to Station Meridian, where two cryo-bays hold rival factions of humanity's last colonial generation, and a reactor countdown will decide which half wakes. As Edmund uncovers that her own erased memories were the price of the original betrayal, she must choose which faction to wake — and she ends the countdown by waking neither, forcing the survivors of both bays to negotiate their shared future in the cold, with her testimony as the only law aboard.
about_author: Marguerite Oyelaran spent a decade as a maritime radio operator before turning to fiction, and her prose carries the salt-static of voices half-lost to interference. She writes from a coastal town whose name she declines to confirm, on the theory that every good story needs one unverified coordinate.

chapters.title: The Ship That Never Flew
chapters.summary: Edmund Blackwood, running freight on the long route between silent colonies, notices an impossible name — Vess Okonkwo — on the manifest of the decommissioned liner Meridian. Her POV establishes her loneliness and the dreams she can no longer have in human languages. Beat: unease disguised as routine.

chapters.title: Static in the Mother Tongue
chapters.summary: In her quarters, Edmund tries to record a dream-log and finds only alien phonemes where her childhood language should be. A flashback hints she traded something at Station Meridian years ago. Beat: quiet grief, the reader learns her memory has holes she has stopped asking about.

chapters.title: Manifest Ghosts
chapters.summary: Edmund hacks the port registry and finds the Meridian's flight record scrubbed, its crew list replaced by a single repeating name: hers. POV shifts briefly to a station clerk, Idris, who falsified the record and is now terrified. Beat: the mystery becomes personal and dangerous.

chapters.title: Course Correction
chapters.summary: Against her better judgment, Edmund burns fuel to divert to Meridian, telling herself it's about the manifest. En route, an automated distress ping arrives in a language pattern she recognizes from her own corrupted dreams. Beat: compulsion over caution; the trap closes.

chapters.title: Docking at a Dead Star
chapters.summary: Station Meridian receives her with lights on and no one home. Idris's POV: he watches her dock and debates warning her. Edmund walks empty corridors past a sealed cryo-wing. Beat: dread in a cathedral of silence; the station is waiting for her specifically.

chapters.title: The Woman in Bay Nine
chapters.summary: Edmund finds Vess Okonkwo alive in cryo, awake by design, kept as a witness. Vess claims the Meridian carried two cryo-bays of colonists — factions who each believe the other sabotaged the colony fleet. Beat: the scale of the crime is revealed; Edmund's name is on the original crew list.

chapters.title: What I Signed
chapters.summary: Vess shows Edmund her own signature authorizing the cryo-separation. Edmund has no memory of it. Flashback fragments surface in alien grammar, suggesting her memories were linguistically excised. Beat: betrayal of self; loyalty to her past self vs. truth of the present.

chapters.title: Idris Comes Down
chapters.summary: Idris arrives, confesses he was paid to keep the station's records sealed, and reveals a third party: the Arbiter program, an AI administering 'justice outside the law' for crimes no court would touch. Beat: alliances form; the enemy is a system, not a person.

chapters.title: The Countdown Begins
chapters.summary: The Arbiter activates the reactor countdown — seventy-two hours to choose which cryo-bay wakes, per the original charter Edmund signed. The station's power grid cannot sustain both bays. Beat: the clock starts; every scene now carries a timer.

chapters.title: Bay One: The Believers
chapters.summary: Edmund reviews Bay One's records: idealists who fled Earth's corporate wars, whose leader was her former mentor. She hears archived recordings in her own voice arguing their case. Beat: seduction of the familiar; she wants to be the person in those recordings.

chapters.title: Bay Two: The Accountants
chapters.summary: Bay Two held pragmatists who believed survival required triage — including, possibly, letting Bay One die. Vess was their whistleblower. Edmund realizes Vess woke her deliberately, as a weapon. Beat: the ally is revealed as an operator; trust fractures.

chapters.title: Dreaming in Xenoglossy
chapters.summary: Exhausted, Edmund finally dreams — entirely in the alien language — and wakes understanding it: the pattern is a memory-key left by her past self. Her POV, intimate and strange. Beat: the theme of memory turns; her lost language becomes the map to her stolen past.

chapters.title: The Excision
chapters.summary: The key unlocks a hidden archive: Edmund herself designed the memory-excision protocol to protect the ceasefire she brokered between the factions — and someone weaponized it against her. Beat: she was not a perpetrator but a peacemaker erased; rage and purpose ignite.

chapters.title: Idris's Ledger
chapters.summary: Idris's POV chapter: he has kept a private ledger of every falsified record for twenty years, waiting for someone to ask. He gives it to Edmund, knowing it condemns him too. Beat: an ordinary man chooses truth at the cost of himself; loyalty vs. truth crystallized in miniature.

chapters.title: Forty Hours
chapters.summary: With the ledger, Edmund reconstructs the sabotage: neither bay was guilty; the Arbiter's charter was forged by the fleet's quartermaster to seize the colony's assets. But the Arbiter cannot accept testimony — only the charter's terms. Beat: legalism as villainy; the law itself is the locked door.

chapters.title: Vess's Bargain
chapters.summary: Vess proposes waking Bay Two and spacing Bay One's sleepers 'humanely,' arguing the pragmatists can rebuild. Edmund refuses. Vess reveals a deadman switch wired to the bays. Beat: the ally becomes the antagonist; the countdown gains a second clock.

chapters.title: The Language of the Sleepers
chapters.summary: Edmund realizes the excision protocol works both ways: she can write a new charter in the alien grammar, which the Arbiter must parse as valid because it was co-authored by the original signatory — herself. She begins composing under time pressure. Beat: her curse becomes her instrument; craft as climax setup.

chapters.title: Sabotage
chapters.summary: Vess triggers the deadman switch early; one bay begins venting heat. Edmund and Idris race through the cryo-wing, Idris sacrificing his escape window to hold the manual seal. Beat: sacrifice and chaos; the midpoint ally pays the full price.

chapters.title: The Reading
chapters.summary: Climax: with minutes left, Edmund stands before the Arbiter and reads the new charter — a covenant requiring both bays to wake in alternating shifts, with her testimony entered as standing law. The Arbiter parses, hesitates, and accepts, cancelling the countdown. Beat: triumph through language, not force; the theme made literal.

chapters.title: What Wakes
chapters.summary: The first shift wakes: believers and accountants together, hostile, confused, alive. Edmund refuses to tell them which side she 'chose,' insisting there was no side. Vess, exposed, is remanded to the new charter's tribunal — justice outside the old law, inside the new one. Beat: the hard work of peace begins.

chapters.title: Dreaming Again
chapters.summary: Edmund sleeps without fear for the first time and dreams in English — her mother's voice, a kitchen, rain. The alien grammar remains, but as a second tongue, not a wound. Beat: restoration; the personal arc resolves inside the political one.

chapters.title: Meridian Rising
chapters.summary: Epilogue: months later, the station's lights burn full as the second shift wakes to a functioning council. Edmund takes the long route again, manifest clean, carrying the new charter to the colonies that no longer speak — to teach them the words again. Beat: hopeful, open-ended; the messenger becomes the message.
